title: Do You Need Shin Guards and Knee Pads for Short Track Speed Skating?
thumbnail_text: Is there a gap in your leg protection?

scenes.heading: Shin Guards and Knee Pads for Short Track
scenes.sub: What each layer does, how to fit it, and the gap check
scenes.narration: Do you need shin guards and knee pads for short track speed skating? Yes, in some form, and you will learn which form, how to fit it, and how to find the gap most skaters leave open. Most national federations require cut resistant protection for competition. Whether you must also wear separate hard pads depends on your federation and your event. So that part of the answer lives in your own rulebook. What almost nobody checks is the join. Plenty of club skaters own decent pads. They still step on with a strip of bare lycra between the boot cuff and the bottom of the shin guard. That is exactly the height a blade travels at when the skater in front goes down.

scenes.heading: Why your legs are so exposed
scenes.chapter: What short track asks of your legs
bullets: Deep crouch puts the shin forward
Kneecap leads through every corner
Falls happen inside a pack
Protection has two jobs, cut and impact
scenes.narration: Your lower legs sit in the most exposed position in the sport. You skate in a deep crouch, so your shin is angled forward and leading. You corner with the knee tracking out over the toe. That makes your kneecap the furthest forward point of your body for most of the lap. And you do all of this inside a pack, where one fall can bring several skaters down with sharp blades still turning. That is why leg protection has two jobs. It has to resist a slicing edge, which is what cut resistant fabric does. And it has to spread a blunt impact, which is what a hard shell or dense foam pad does. Kit that does only one of those leaves half the problem open.

scenes.heading: The coverage chain and its two gaps
scenes.narration: Think of your leg protection as one continuous surface. At the top, knee protection covers the whole kneecap, not just the top half. Below it, shin protection runs down the front of the shin and overlaps both the sock and the knee pad. The chain breaks in two places. Gap one sits between the knee pad and the shin guard, and it opens up when you bend. Gap two sits between the shin guard and the top of the boot. That is the one most skaters leave open. Check both gaps in a deep skating position, not standing upright.

scenes.heading: Can you use football shin guards?
bullets: Fine for training, better than nothing
Often too short to meet the knee pad
Slide when held up by a sock alone
Wear them over a cut resistant layer
scenes.narration: This is the real question behind most searches, and for training the answer is usually yes. A hard shell football guard covers the front of the shin, survives a long time and is easy to replace. If that is what you own, use it rather than skating with nothing. Know the limits, though. Football guards are cut for a low boot, so the top often finishes well below your knee pad. A guard held up only by a sock slides sideways when you slide across the ice. Guards with their own sleeve or strap behave far better. Most important, the plastic shell does nothing for the calf and the sides of the leg. So wear a football guard over a cut resistant layer, never instead of one. And check your competition rules before you race in them.

scenes.heading: Fabric layer or hard pads?
scenes.chapter: Built into the suit or separate pads
bullets: Fabric resists a blade, whole leg
Pads spread impact, front only
Fabric adds no bulk under the suit
Most skaters run some of each
scenes.narration: Protection for the legs comes two ways. Cut resistant fabric comes as part of a suit, so it is there every time you get dressed. It covers the whole leg, including the back of the calf, depending on the garment. But it spreads very little impact. A hard pad spreads impact well, but only across the front of the shin and the kneecap. Many sports pads are not cut resistant at all. These are not really alternatives, because they solve different problems. If you are new and falling often, run both, with proper pads over the fabric. A bruised kneecap keeps you off the ice longer than a scuffed suit. As your falls get rarer but faster, slim pads become easier to live with than bulky shells.

scenes.heading: Fitting a knee pad
bullets: Set it with the knee bent
Bend to your cornering angle
Centre the pad on the kneecap
Stand up and watch it move
scenes.narration: A pad only protects the skin it is sitting on when you hit the ice. And where it sits in the changing room is not where it sits at the end of a slide. So set knee protection with your leg bent, not straight. Fit it standing upright and it will ride up your thigh the moment you drop into position. That leaves the joint open. Bend your knee to roughly the angle you corner at. Centre the pad on the cap. Then stand up and watch where it travels. If it moves more than a little, the strap is too loose or the pad is too big.

scenes.heading: Where a knee pad has to sit
scenes.narration: Here are two knees side by side. On the left, the pad is centred on the kneecap. It was set with the knee bent and then checked standing. This pad covers the joint that hits the ice first. On the right, the pad has ridden up the thigh. The kneecap underneath is left open, and that is what lands first when you go down forwards. A pad in that position is protecting your thigh, which was never the problem.

scenes.heading: Shin protection: overlap, not touch
bullets: Work upwards from the boot
Pull cut resistant socks up high
Guard overlaps the sock top
Touching pieces separate when you flex
scenes.narration: For shin protection, work upwards from the boot. Pull your cut resistant socks up as high as they go. Look at where the gripper band finishes against your boot cuff, because that varies with the boot and the sock. If the sock clears the cuff, set the shin guard so its lower edge overlaps the sock rather than starting above it. If it does not clear the cuff, that bare band is a gap you need to close another way. Overlap is the whole point. Two pieces that just touch while you stand will separate by a finger width as soon as you flex your ankle forward. The same is true where the guard meets the knee pad.

scenes.heading: The fifteen second gap check
bullets: Boot line: any bare skin?
Sock top: guard overlapping it?
Guard to knee: still overlapping?
Kneecap: pad still centred?
scenes.narration: This check takes fifteen seconds. Get into your lowest skating position in front of a mirror. Look down the front of both legs and work through four points. First, the boot line. Is there bare skin or plain lycra between the boot and the shin guard? Second, the sock top. Is the guard overlapping the cut resistant sock, rather than starting above it? Third, guard to knee. With your knee bent, does the shin guard still overlap the knee pad? Fourth, the kneecap. Is the pad centred on the cap in this position, not parked on your thigh? There is usually a gap the first time anyone does this. It is almost always at the boot line. Fix it there, not in a pile up.

scenes.heading: Choosing pads that work
scenes.chapter: What to look for in pads
bullets: Its own sleeve or a real strap
Slim enough for under the race suit
Shell covers the whole kneecap
Never size up to grow into
scenes.narration: LiveLica stocks the cut resistant foundation, such as undersuits and ankle socks, but not hard shin guards or knee pads. So here is what to look for when you buy pads elsewhere. Choose a pad that has its own sleeve or a real strap, so it does not rely on a sock. Choose one slim enough to fit under a race suit without bunching. Pads go under the suit and over your cut resistant base layer, never on the outside. Check the shell covers the whole kneecap, because the bottom edge of the cap meets the ice first. And for juniors, do not size pads up to grow into. A pad loose enough to last two seasons is loose enough to slide off the cap in a fall.

scenes.heading: When a knock needs more than ice
bullets: Sharp pain, not a dull ache
Clear swelling, numbness or tingling
Cannot put weight through the leg
Deep or bleeding blade cuts, same day
scenes.narration: Most leg contact in short track is a bruise. A bruise usually settles with rest and a few days off hard cornering. Some knocks need more. See a doctor or physiotherapist if you have sharp pain rather than a dull ache. Go if the knee or shin swells noticeably, or if you feel numbness or pins and needles below the point of contact. Go if you cannot put weight through the leg, or if the pain is still there after a few days. And any cut from a blade that is deep, gaping or will not stop bleeding needs medical attention the same day. Not a plaster and the next session.

scenes.heading: Fabric first, pads over it, and close every gap
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: Before your next session, put a cut resistant layer on under your suit and treat it as the foundation. Fit any pad with your knee bent, and make each piece overlap the next rather than just meet. Then do the mirror check in your lowest position and close whatever gap you find. It will probably be at the boot line. Read your own federation's rules for the details, because that part really does vary. The full guide, with the comparison table and common questions, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
